messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 27
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 64

He is 27, a South Eastern Asian man who works as a journalist, and he still remembers how ordinary the beginning of the relationship feels. He meets his partner at a community event he is covering for work. At first, he experiences the attention as flattering. His partner seems protective, intensely interested in his life, waiting up after late assignments, bringing food to the newsroom, asking detailed questions about the people he interviews. He tells himself this is what commitment looks like. When his partner becomes irritated by his long hours, by messages from editors that arrive late at night, by the fact that he sometimes has to leave dinner to follow a story, he explains it away as insecurity.

The first time he is shoved, they are arguing in his apartment about a colleague who has called after midnight. He is so startled that he says nothing for several seconds. His back hits the wall hard enough to leave pain between his shoulders the next morning. His partner cries immediately afterward, says stress has been building, says it will never happen again. He wants to believe that. He has built a career around noticing what other people do not say, around asking hard questions, around seeing patterns, but in his own life he keeps narrowing the frame. He focuses on the apology, the flowers, the tenderness that follows.

Over time, the violence becomes part of the rhythm of the relationship. It is never constant, which makes it easier for him to doubt himself. There are weeks of calm. Then a slammed door, a grabbed wrist, fingers pressing too hard into his upper arm, a blow to the side of his head when he tries to walk away. Once, his partner locks him in the bathroom for nearly an hour while accusing him of cheating with a source. He sits on the closed toilet lid, staring at the tile, aware of his own heartbeat in his throat. He thinks with humiliating clarity that if he says the right thing, if he stays very still, if he does not provoke anything, this will end faster.

He becomes skilled at concealment. As a journalist, he is often around people who notice details, so he learns to get ahead of their questions. A bruise near his collarbone becomes “a clumsy run-in with a shelf.” A split lip is blamed on rushing to catch the train. He stops changing clothes at the gym because he does not want anyone to see the marks on his ribs. He writes sharply observed pieces about city politics and labor disputes while privately organizing his life around someone else’s moods. He keeps his phone on silent during interviews, but his attention drifts anyway. If too many messages pile up from his partner, his stomach drops and his palms sweat. He starts checking the screen between questions, then hates himself for losing the thread of a conversation.

The final assault happens after he returns home later than expected from covering a protest. His partner has been calling for an hour. The apartment is dark except for the kitchen light. He knows from the silence, before a word is spoken, that something is wrong. The argument turns quickly. His partner accuses him of lying, of being with someone else, of choosing work over the relationship. When he tries to move past him, he is hit in the face and knocked sideways into the counter. He remembers the metallic taste in his mouth, the shock of seeing blood drip onto the floor, the strange detached thought that he should document this, like evidence. Instead he freezes. He hears himself apologizing though he does not know for what. A neighbor eventually bangs on the wall, and the interruption breaks something open in him. The next morning, while his partner is out, he leaves with a backpack, his laptop, and the notebook he has been carrying all week.

Since then, the danger has ended, but his body does not seem to believe it. In the present, he lives with his girlfriend, who is patient and careful, and he hates how often he startles when she enters a room unexpectedly. If she reaches for him from behind while he is washing dishes, his shoulders jump and his whole body goes tight before he can stop it. He is ashamed of the fear because she has never hurt him. At night he sleeps lightly, waking at small sounds in the hallway. Some nights he dreams he is back in the apartment kitchen, unable to move, trying to speak through a swollen mouth. He wakes already braced, heart racing, scanning the room.

His work has changed too. Assignments that once energized him now drain him. He can still perform—he meets deadlines, asks smart questions, files clean copy—but crowded press scrums and angry confrontations leave him shaky afterward. If an interview subject raises his voice, even in ordinary frustration, he loses the next few seconds. He feels himself disappear inward, vision narrowing, ears filled with static. On trains he chooses a seat near the door. In restaurants he tracks exits without meaning to. He avoids the neighborhood where his former partner lived, and when he receives messages from unknown numbers, he lets them sit unanswered for hours.

What troubles him most is how thoroughly the experience has altered his sense of himself. He used to think of himself as observant, composed, hard to rattle. Now he second-guesses his reactions constantly. He wonders why he stayed, why he minimized, why he still feels afraid when the person who hurt him is no longer in his home. He speaks about these questions quietly, with long pauses, as if each one costs him something. Even in moments of safety, part of him remains prepared for impact.
